#5343. Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents

Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.

The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.

The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.

Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.

Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.

For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.

I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format, with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.

It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.

“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.

Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.

Aina’s ring goes on preorder starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.

XRP’s leveraged market went through a series of brutal flushes this week. In just five days, derivative traders who bet on the token’s upside have lost more than $30 million, according to CoinGlass. What happened is a sudden price reversal after a moment of optimism on November 4 that caught buyers off guard and set off a cascade of liquidations all across the crypto board.

Liquidations hit extreme levels by Friday, running 2.74 times above the weekly average. Exchanges' data shows a completely lopsided picture where longs account for 95.54% of all daily losses worth $16.01 million out of a total $16.75 million. Shorts got off with a scare, losing a token $746,000. Of course, Binance as the most liquid platform was the place of the most pain, with $8.06 million in leveraged positions on XRP wiped out on the exchange.

What played out is a textbook long squeeze. Traders opened overleveraged positions hoping the rally would continue, got trapped in a falling trend, and their forced closures started knocking each other out down the chain. More than 3,600 traders worldwide lost their deposits completely.

XRP dropped 6.41% over the past days on the spot market, leaving the price pinned at $1.1799 by the weekend. How strong sellers are is evident by the XRP/USD chart on TradingView. Here the weekly candle comes to closure with a long upper wick, meaning every bullish attempt to take control and buy the dip above $1.22 was shut down.

#5341. Exclusive: Nubank Alum Raises $14M For Colombia’s Palomma To Tackle Rent Payments, Landlord Financing

In 2020, Cipriano Echavarría was working at Morgan Stanley in New York and weighing his next career move when he noticed a plaque on his desk. Among the names of people who had sat there before him was David Vélez.

He looked up the name. Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank. Echavarría took a photo of the plaque and messaged him on LinkedIn, asking for career advice.

It turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with plans to eventually start a company of his own.

Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma, has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned.

The financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital, Clocktower Technology Ventures, Tekton Ventures, Simma Capital and Yango Ventures, alongside existing investors Y Combinator, 17Sigma, Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures.

Palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume.

The company will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría said Colombia remains the priority.

“We want to win Colombia,” he said in an interview.

Palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners.

After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, MIT-trained engineers with experience at Meta, Cobre and JP Morgan. The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent.

It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said.

Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties.

The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled.

Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the company a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products.

From there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and credit-building benefits, while Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront. Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults. The company is also developing Palomma Flex, which would let tenants split their monthly rent into two installments.

Property managers pay a subscription fee for the AI software, and Palomma earns a percentage of rent through its payments and financial services.

Getting customers to adopt more of its services has helped drive Palomma’s growth. The company reports net revenue retention of 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from an existing group of customers nearly quadrupled, even after accounting for customers who left or spent less.

Overall, the decision to combine AI leasing software, payments and financial services reflects Echavarría’s view of what it takes to build a large business in Latin America. He pointed to U.S. companies such as EliseAI, Bilt, TheGuarantors and Flex as comparisons for different parts of Palomma’s business.  Echavarría believes that reaching a similar scale in Latin America requires a wider range of products.

“In the U.S., you can build one solution and be really large because the market allows it,” he said. “In Latin America, if you want to be really large, you need to do all the things.”

AI also helps decide which tenants qualify for rental guarantees. Palomma’s leasing agent communicates through WhatsApp and collects application documents. The company claims that it can then deliver an approval in under 30 seconds. The company draws on information from leasing conversations and rental payment behavior to assess applicants.

The company’s rental guarantees put Palomma on the hook if tenants don’t pay. The startup initially takes on that risk itself, but Echavarría told Crunchbase News it was working to finalize a partnership with an insurer that would share the risk and let Palomma offer more guarantees.

The startup is also using AI to keep its team small. As of Nov. 4, it had 18 employees, up from about 14 when it closed its Series A roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer service employee works alongside AI agents to support the roughly 200,000 tenants paying rent through Palomma’s platform, Echavarría said.

The startup operates on the premise that AI can make real estate financial services cheaper to provide, much as mobile technology helped digital banks compete with lenders that maintained large branch networks. Longer term, Palomma also plans to expand beyond rentals into homeowners association payments and residential property transactions.

Pepe Bolaños, managing partner at Cometa, said Palomma stood out for its founding team and the opportunity to modernize Latin America’s fragmented rental market. In Colombia alone, nearly 8 million households rent their homes, he noted.

“We look for companies tackling markets where outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset that can be leveraged and monetized through AI,” he wrote via email.

Bolaños pointed to Echavarría’s experience helping scale Nubank, and Monsalve and del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds. In roughly 18 months, Palomma grew to process around $130 million in monthly rental payments and serve more than 200,000 tenants with about 14 employees, he said.

“That kind of execution is unusual. It convinced us that this team has what it takes to build a much larger business,” he added.

Unlike competitors focused on individual services, Palomma combines rent collection, tenant screening and rental guarantees, gathering data throughout the process, Bolaños said. Directly processing payments gives it insight into tenant behavior that can improve underwriting, flag potential defaults and support new financial products, while AI helps automate operations.

“We believe the combination of distribution, proprietary payment data and AI gives Palomma a competitive advantage that can become stronger as the company grows,” he said.

#5340. Zipline hits $21.5B valuation as Walmart expands bet on drone delivery

Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.

Zipline and Walmart reached a new multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.

On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.

The company, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, said it plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.

Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based company began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.

But it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.

Zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.

The company said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

Just about a week after Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao's brief banter with Elon Musk over his unsettling humor about Binance's recent $6 billion attack, another rumor about Musk's comment on the exchange surfaced again.

While the claims had come amid growing speculation about Elon Musk making peace with CZ, the post had immediately gone viral, receiving mixed reactions from the crypto community.

While the post claimed that billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk criticized Binance for its dominance in the crypto market, CZ dismissed the claims, calling out the poster for spreading misleading information.

Notably, the post claimed that Musk had questioned Binance's alleged 80% market share, arguing that its dominance was limiting competition within the crypto industry.

Moreover, the poster added that Musk had advised crypto users to move their funds to alternative exchanges to encourage competition, suggesting that such a move could potentially create the opportunity for another bull run.

Nonetheless, CZ debunked the information, declaring it false while issuing a subtle warning to the poster about spreading information that is not true.

After CZ declared the information to be false, he further backed his response with proof from an AI search, which clearly showed the falseness of the claims.

Notably, CZ shared a screenshot of the AI search result that disputed the alleged comments, stating that no original post from Musk could be found supporting the claims about Binance's 80% market share.

It also mentioned that Elon Musk did not encourage users to move their funds to competing exchanges either.

A few hours after CZ dismissed the false claims, Elon Musk also joined in, testifying that he never said any of the things mentioned in the post.

As proven by CZ's AI search, Musk acknowledged that the post was fabricated, backing CZ's response.

#5338. Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscriptsclaiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.

Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.

On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.

Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.

The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.

Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.

Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.

For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.

That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.

“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”

The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.

“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.

To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”

Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.

The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan said.

Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.”

Axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”

Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.

Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.

“We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan said. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”

The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.

“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong said. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”

Hong is confident enough in that approach to issue a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”

#5336. Food delivery startup Wonder files for IPO as it explores its next big bite

Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.

Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.

Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.

Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.

Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.

Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.

Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.

Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.

Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

According to him, the behavior has become disruptive enough that he now has to block some of those accounts, as he explained that the replies not only affect his interactions but also inconvenience other X users whose posts he engages with.

Schwartz considers this conduct very concerning, as flooding unrelated conversations with XRP content or personal attacks can force the people he is responding to to block him to prevent their followers from receiving irrelevant notifications.

In his post, Schwartz further spotlighted the increasing fraud allegations he has continued to receive on his unrelated posts, revealing plans to take action on that as well.

He mentioned that he will block the accounts of users who follow him across X to accuse him of fraud or scamming, whether their comments are positive or negative.

While expressing his displeasure, Schwartz warned that he would not tolerate people using his participation in other users' discussions as an opportunity to promote XRP or attack him.

#5334. Harbinger raises $240M after expanding into defense

Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.

The funding comes almost one year to the day after the Los Angeles-based company announced a $160 million Series C, which included an initial truck order from FedEx. Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

The Series D was co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s “technology impact fund,” and defense-focused firm Ridgeline. The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors. FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.

Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis. The company has steadily expanded its efforts since. It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI, has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles, and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.

#5333. webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card shows the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 new tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

The card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

Perplexity AI predicts what the US CPI data may read and, if so, what could potentially happen to Bitcoin and the broader market. CPI data remains one of the most market-moving economic releases for both stocks and crypto. The next one is in two days, on November 10, and both crypto and the stock market seem to be waiting to see which direction it goes from here.

Traditionally, a cooler-than-expected Consumer Price Index print is bullish for risk assets. Lower inflation reduces pressure on the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates elevated or hike them further, which supports lower Treasury yields, a softer dollar, and higher valuations for growth-oriented assets.

The inflation rate increased in September on the back of higher gasoline and energy prices amid the Iran war, further squeezing households’ budgets and perhaps pressuring the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, economists said.

The consumer price index rose by 3.7% in September from 12 months earlier, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. That’s up from 3.4% annually in August.

September’s report came in hotter than expected, triggering an immediate sell-off across cryptocurrency and broader risk-asset markets.

Bitcoin slid from roughly $83,900–$84,000 down toward $81,000–$81,500, hitting lows around $80,210 in subsequent early trading sessions.

The total cryptocurrency market capitalization compressed to $2.7 trillion, accompanied by over $160M in leveraged long liquidations within a 24-hour window following the October 14 CPI data drop.

Equities, particularly the Nasdaq and rate-sensitive sectors, tend to rally as the discount rate on future earnings declines. Crypto often amplifies this reaction: Bitcoin and major altcoins historically perform well in environments of easing monetary expectations because they benefit from improved liquidity conditions and renewed risk appetite.

Conversely, a hotter-than-expected CPI reading typically pressures stocks and crypto lower, reinforcing a “higher-for-longer” rates narrative, strengthening the dollar, and lifting yields.

For the October 2026 CPI data due Tuesday, November 10 at 8:30 a.m. ET, current market consensus points to a clear cooling from September’s strong print.

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg and other sources expect headline CPI to rise 0.3% month-over-month (down from +0.6% previously), with core CPI (excluding food and energy) advancing 0.2% MoM (down from +0.3%).

Some forecasts cluster slightly lower around 0.2–0.25% for headline. Year-over-year figures are complicated by prior data gaps, but the monthly numbers are the primary focus.

Sentiment leans toward a soft-to-in-line outcome that would confirm inflation is decelerating after two firmer months, though markets remain sensitive to any upside surprise in core services or shelter components.

Perplexity AI predicts a modestly softer print than the median consensus: headline CPI at +0.2% MoM and core CPI at +0.2% MoM. This would represent a more pronounced cooling than many expect, driven by slower energy contribution, softer used-vehicle prices, and some moderation in owners’ equivalent rent after recent spikes.

While not a dramatic undershoot, it would land on the dovish side of the range. If this prediction materializes, risk assets should react positively. Treasury yields would likely dip, the dollar could soften, and both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would find support for a relief rally.

Crypto would stand to benefit disproportionately in the short term, with Bitcoin potentially extending recent recovery gains and higher-beta alts seeing stronger percentage moves as liquidity expectations improve.

A confirmatory soft print would also increase the odds that the Federal Reserve maintains a more patient stance into the December meeting, reducing near-term hawkish risks.

However, the market impact would still depend on the details, particularly the composition of core inflation, and any accompanying commentary on sticky services categories. Overall, a result in line with or slightly below the Perplexity forecast would reinforce the recent post-midterm risk-on tone rather than derail it.

Bitcoin is now trading around $73,600 after briefly losing the $73,000 level. Ethereum slipped below $2,100, while XRP approached $1.05 and Solana struggled to hold $82. More than $723 million in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with nearly 79% coming from long bets.

October’s hotter-than-expected US inflation report has revived concerns about interest rates, while recent US election results have introduced another layer of regulatory uncertainty. The interest-rate outlook has become even more concerning. The combination of ETF withdrawals, leveraged liquidations and inflation uncertainty has created a difficult environment for buyers. Social chatter has pushed back against describing the move as a full-blown crash, pointing to comparisons with the Nasdaq’s monthly decline. Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation. #5325. After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a new operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.

McMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks. The software is expected to launch in 2027 as a free-to-use desktop operating system, with support for existing Intel- and AMD-powered PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. McMaster told TechCrunch that these tools have accelerated development by at least fivefold, with most of the gains coming over the past six months.

Microsoft has long dominated the PC operating-system market, making it hard for newer players to establish a foothold. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple’s OS X, according to Statcounter’s web traffic data.

However, McMaster believes Kora does not need to compete for Windows’ entire user base. Rather, he is targeting people who use AI extensively and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services.

“Microsoft can keep its billion users,” McMaster said, estimating that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue. He expects that market to exceed 200 million users by 2033.

McMaster told TechCrunch that his experience at Cyanogen, where he spent over five years, taught him the dangers of relying on the very company he was trying to challenge. Cyanogen remained heavily dependent on Google Mobile Services despite offering features beyond Google’s version of Android. That ultimately restricted its ability to build an independent ecosystem.

“If you are trying to compete with an incumbent but are still reliant on them, you have no chance,” he said.

Kora, McMaster said, builds on an idea he pursued toward the end of his time at Cyanogen, when he began exploring ways to integrate third-party services directly into the operating system. With Kora, he wants AI models and agents to work across applications and access files without being confined to individual apps.

Previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system company led by McMaster, the Palo Alto-based company rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted its focus to AI. The decision came as early companies, including Perplexity and OpenAI, were moving into AI-powered web browsers, McMaster said. He believed browsers would not give AI agents enough access to a computer to carry out more complex tasks, making an operating system a better starting point.

The shift also allowed Kora to build on nearly three years of work developing Playtron’s Linux-based gaming operating system, called GameOS, instead of starting from scratch.

Kora is designed to let users work with different AI models and agents across applications, while keeping track of conversations, documents, and other information. It also allows AI agents to operate in separate workspaces with restricted access to files and other resources.

While McMaster has drawn on his experience at Cyanogen, none of Kora’s engineers worked there. Instead, the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community, he told TechCrunch.

Kora’s software is built on Linux and uses Nix. It replaces the Fedora Silverblue foundation of Playtron’s earlier GameOS.

While Linux and Nix are open source, McMaster said Kora’s own technology, including its Cortex AI engine and desktop interface, remains proprietary. The company, he said, intends to support AI models and services from different providers, although it has not committed to making its own software open source.

Gaming also remains part of Kora’s plans. McMaster said the company intends to introduce AI-powered tools that would allow developers to create, publish, and play games directly within the operating system. He added that support for Android apps is also on its roadmap.

McMaster told TechCrunch that Kora’s team has worked closely with Qualcomm’s engineers for nearly a year to optimize the operating system specifically for Snapdragon-powered PCs. The collaboration includes support for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips.

Alongside Qualcomm, Kora is working with Saudi Arabia’s AI company Humain on an enterprise version of the operating system, called Humain OS, which is expected to run on Snapdragon-powered laptops in 2027. Kora also plans to announce partnerships with PC manufacturers at a later date, though McMaster did not identify any companies or provide a specific timeline.

Kora plans to generate revenue through subscriptions that bundle access to AI models and agentic services. Moreover, its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and use cloud-based models for work requiring more computing power.

Kora’s investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which previously backed Playtron. The company, McMaster said, has raised additional funding since shifting its focus to AI. However, he declined to disclose the total amount raised or its valuation. Kora has enough funding to operate for several years, he said.

Bitcoin closed the week below its 50-week moving average for the first time in two months, just as warnings grow that the calm in the oil market may not last.

The weekly candle closed at $74,851 at midnight UTC on Sunday. That is below the 50-week simple moving average (MA), the average of the last 50 weekly closes, which sits at $75,535. It was also the fifth losing week in a row, and BTC trades at $74,312 on Binance on Monday morning.

Oil has gone the other way. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell 17% from $117.64 on October 30 to $97.35 this morning, as traders bet on a deal to end the war with Iran.

That bet may be early. Amos Hochstein was an energy adviser to President Joe Biden. He told CNBC that the risk of renewed war is “still alive.” If fighting resumes, he said, gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel prices would all surge.

So if oil spikes again, does BTC fall further?

The drop came fast. Brent lost 10.9% on Monday, November 2, and another 8.7% on Wednesday, as traders bet that the fighting would end.

No deal has been signed. Late Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it had disabled a tanker that ignored warnings after visiting an Iranian port, and attacks on tankers near Oman have continued since the U.S. election.

Others see the same risk. Rapidan Energy, an energy consulting firm, puts the chance that fighting resumes at 80%. Its president, Bob McNally, expects crude to climb back above $100 a barrel if it does.

The pattern since the spring is clear enough to watch. We matched every Brent trading day since March 2 with BTC’s move on the same date, 176 days in all.

Last week showed both sides. On Wednesday, Brent fell 8.7%, and BTC rose 3.9%. On Thursday, Brent rose 3.9%, while BTC fell 5.5%.

The link is loose, not fixed. Both prices react to the same war headlines, and on a third of the big oil-up days, BTC still rose. The timing is also approximate, because Brent settles in New York while Binance’s daily candle closes at midnight UTC.

Still, a renewed oil spike would hit BTC at a weak moment, with the price already below its long-term average.

#5322. Why Bitcoin, Nasdaq, AI Stocks, and Chips Move Together? The Liquidity Machine Explained

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin can fall alongside Nvidia, and Nasdaq can rally while Ethereum follows. Semiconductor stocks can plunge as investors reassess AI spending, dragging crypto sentiment down with them. These markets appear to have little in common. Bitcoin was designed outside traditional banking, while chipmakers supply the infrastructure powering artificial intelligence.

Yet they increasingly respond to the same financial force: liquidity.

The Federal Reserve, US Treasury, Wall Street, and institutional investors form a financial network connecting these seemingly unrelated markets. Understanding that network explains why everything from Bitcoin and Ethereum to Nvidia, TSMC, and AI infrastructure can move together.

The Federal Reserve sits near the center of this relationship. Its interest rate decisions influence borrowing costs, bond yields, financing conditions, and investor appetite for risk.

When interest rates fall, investors generally become more comfortable holding riskier assets. Cheaper financing can support technology valuations, speculative investments, and crypto demand. When rates rise, the opposite can happen. Investors reassess expensive valuations, reduce leverage, and move toward safer assets.

Quantitative tightening adds another layer, and here’s why: the Fed reduces its balance sheet, and Treasury securities return to private investors. This can reduce available reserves and put pressure on short-term funding markets.

The US Treasury also influences liquidity through government borrowing and its Treasury General Account. Large changes in government cash balances can affect money circulating through the banking system.

Banks, money-market funds, hedge funds and primary dealers connect these policies to financial markets. Repo financing, Treasury yields and institutional funding costs help determine how much capital investors can deploy.

The Federal Reserve’s August 2026 research examined these connections directly. It found that Treasury issuance and dealer holdings can put upward pressure on repo rates.

“The overnight Treasury repo market is one of the most important funding markets in the world. It sees more than $8 trillion in daily trading volume and plays a vital role in broader Treasury market liquidity and price discovery.3 Repo rates also determine the secured overnight financing rate (SOFR)—now the primary reference rate for trillions of dollars of financial contracts—thereby affecting broader financial conditions.” – Fed’s Research

This is why Bitcoin does not need a Federal Reserve policy change to affect its network. A change in financing conditions can influence investors holding Bitcoin, Nasdaq stocks, and other risky assets simultaneously.

Artificial intelligence has created one of the largest investment cycles in modern technology. But the boom extends far beyond software companies. Nvidia supplies GPUs powering AI infrastructure. AMD competes in accelerated computing, while Broadcom supplies networking and custom silicon.

TSMC manufactures advanced chips used across the industry. ASML supplies the lithography equipment needed to produce increasingly sophisticated semiconductors. Samsung and Intel also compete across memory, manufacturing and chip technology. These companies sit at the beginning of an enormous infrastructure spending cycle.

Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle are investing heavily in data centers, cloud computing, power infrastructure and AI capacity. This spending requires capital from multiple sources. Companies issue bonds, borrow from banks, tap private credit and use operating cash flows to finance expansion.

Reuters reported on November 6 that US investment-grade corporate bond issuance reached $1.88 trillion through November 4. Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle raised more than $370.7 billion as they financed AI and data-center investment.

Goldman Sachs expects bonds to fund 35% of hyperscalers’ capital expenditure in 2027. The consequences extend across financial markets. Investors buying AI-related stocks, semiconductor shares and corporate bonds must constantly reassess financing costs and expected returns.

Equity capital will continue to play a supporting role in funding the AI investment boom in 2027.Hyperscalers and other AI infrastructure companies accounted for roughly $65 billion in follow-on issuance (post-IPO equity offerings) this year, around 45% of the US total.In… https://t.co/O9UBnu9S1Z pic.twitter.com/jsBX59xJnw

When investors question AI valuations or the profitability of massive data-center investments, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and their customers can face selling pressure.

That same risk-off sentiment can reach Bitcoin, Ethereum and speculative altcoins. Hedge funds and institutional investors may reduce exposure across several asset classes simultaneously.

The connection is not that Bitcoin depends on Nvidia’s earnings. Both markets are exposed to changes in capital availability, leverage, and investor confidence.

Institutional adoption has fundamentally changed how crypto like Bitcoin markets interact with traditional finance like Nasdaq. BlackRock, Fidelity, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and other financial institutions now participate in digital asset markets through investment products, custody, trading, and infrastructure.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs have created another channel between traditional portfolios and crypto prices. When institutional investors adjust their allocations, those flows can influence Bitcoin demand.

Meanwhile, stablecoins connect crypto directly to traditional money markets. Tether and Circle issue dollar-backed stablecoins supported by reserve assets, including US Treasury securities. Their growing importance creates another link between government debt markets and crypto liquidity.

BREAKING: The total circulating supply of onchain tokenized equities surged by +$932 million last week, the biggest weekly jump on record.This puts total supply above $4.7 billion, also a fresh record high.Amid the US Midterm elections and the resulting volatility, tokenized… pic.twitter.com/nkAMG23PJv

Tokenized stocks and Treasury products push this integration further. The SEC issued guidance on tokenized securities in January 2026, clarifying how existing securities laws apply to blockchain-based ownership structures. In September, it also introduced temporary conditional exemptions facilitating certain tokenized stock trading venues.

The Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation (DTCC) is another important player in modernizing securities infrastructure through tokenization. Coinbase, Binance, and other crypto exchanges provide additional trading infrastructure connecting digital assets with global capital.

The irony is difficult to ignore. Bitcoin was created after the 2008 financial crisis as an alternative to central banks and traditional monetary systems. Yet its growing institutional ownership has exposed its market price to many of the same forces driving Wall Street.

The important gap is between Bitcoin’s technology and its financial market behavior. Bitcoin’s decentralized network still operates independently of the Federal Reserve. Its supply schedule does not change when Nvidia rallies or Treasury yields increase.

However, its market price is increasingly influenced by institutional positioning, leverage, ETF flows, and global risk appetite.

CME Group research found Bitcoin’s correlation with the Nasdaq-100 increased from virtually zero during 2014–2019 to 0.42 during 2020–2022. Its correlation remained around 0.30 between 2023 and April 2025. CME research also found crypto assets sometimes reached correlations of 0.35–0.60 with the Nasdaq during 2025 and early 2026.

This does not mean Bitcoin has become another technology stock. Correlation measures price behavior, not the underlying purpose or value of an asset.

But it raises an important question about Bitcoin’s original mission:

If Bitcoin rises when Wall Street has abundant liquidity and falls when institutional investors reduce risk, how independent is its market value from traditional finance?

#5321. PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.

“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”

The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.

The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.

More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.

“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”

That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.

“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”

For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.

“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”

Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.

“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.

“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”

As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.

“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”

“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

#5320. Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

BNB Chain has launched a new security feature, "Red Alarm," to help users identify potentially risky decentralized applications (dApps) and smart contracts in its ecosystem.

"Red Alarm" aims to improve user protection by highlighting potentially high-risk dApps and contracts, providing users with more information to consider before interacting with them.

BNB Chain said user safety in the crypto industry is a work in progress, especially as decentralized finance and blockchain applications are on the rise. As more users engage with smart contract systems and decentralized platforms, it has become increasingly important to identify potential security threats.

On November 6, 2026, BNB Chain issued a notice, stating it was aware of the security risk affecting the Reth client. However, its opBNB does not use op-reth, with the impact on BSC-Reth being limited.

It reserves a share of each block's gas capacity for eligible payments, protecting that capacity from general traffic. The default reservation is 5% of each block's gas limit.

Payment Lane sets aside capacity for qualifying BNB transfers between wallets, so unrelated activity cannot use it all. Token payments can also qualify once approved for the lane.

Ripple contributed to a white paper commissioned by the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), which brings together perspectives and  insights from leading practitioners across the financial services ecosystem.

Ripple's Managing Director, Middle East & Africa, Reece Merrick, recently stated his contribution to  the DFSA's new publication: "Scaling Tokenization: The Road Ahead," alongside leaders from BlackRock, Standard Chartered and Robinhood.

The white paper considers the conditions that may support the responsible scaling of tokenised financial assets and related market infrastructure, including within the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC).

Aside from Merrick, other contributors include Tony Ashraf, Managing Director, Head of Technology & Operations and Head of Digital Assets, Middle East & Africa at BlackRock; Coy Garrison, Senior Director and Deputy General Counsel, Crypto at Robinhood; René Michau, Global Head, Digital Asset Advisory at Standard Chartered;  Henson Orser, Founder and Chief  Executive at Soter Insure; and Herman Schueller, Director, Innovation and Technology Risk Supervision at DFSA.

According to the DFSA report, tokenization of traditional financial assets has the potential to become a significant development in mainstream financial markets, offering the prospect of greater access for investors, increased efficiency for issuers and intermediaries, and reduced risk in certain areas, especially around settlement, for the wider financial system.

Merrick shared his perspective, saying that the real shift is not just tokenized treasuries and MMFs (Money Market Funds) gaining AUM but rather their on-chain utility as collateral in repo and margin without needing to redeem to cash first. This viewpoint follows as repo markets continue to move trillions daily, with Merrick highlighting this as potential for tokenization.

Merrick anticipates massive growth in this regard over the next 12 months, predicting that a significant proportion of that will be on the XRP Ledger.

"With clear frameworks, institutional custody, and trusted settlement assets like RLUSD, the UAE, DIFC and Ripple are positioned at the forefront of this next phase," Merrick stated.

Forecasts for the future size of tokenised assets vary considerably. Citi Institute's base case is for the global market in tokenised financial assets to reach $5.5 trillion by 2030.  A Standard Chartered and Synpulse paper estimated that demand for tokenised assets could reach $30.1 trillion by 2034.

The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) has picked Avalanche as the only blockchain to settle tokenized stocks on its planned 24/7 trading platform, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens that track shares of real companies. The NYSE version would let investors trade U.S. stocks around the clock, settle trades instantly and pay with stablecoins, digital tokens that hold a steady $1 value.

The New York Stock Exchange has selected Avalanche ($AVAX) as the exclusive blockchain for settling tokenized U.S. stocks on its upcoming 24/7 trading platform, according to the WSJ.NYSE cited Avalanche’s speed, throughput and compliance capabilities.The platform is targeting… pic.twitter.com/uE4S3X5lnn

AVAX jumped on the news. It rose 4.3% in the minute the reports hit at 12:30 UTC, and it trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% on the day while Bitcoin and Ether are down.

The pick lands on a chain that holds only a small slice of the market today. Avalanche carries $179 million of the $3.73 billion in tokenized shares tracked by rwa.xyz. That is 4.8% of the market, down from 10.3% a month ago.

So can the NYSE deal make Avalanche the main home for these tokens?

The plan is not new, but the blockchain is. NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) first announced the platform in January and said it would seek regulatory approval.

The tokens would not be copies. ICE said they would be interchangeable with ordinary shares and carry the same dividend and voting rights.

NYSE picked Avalanche for its speed, the number of trades it can handle, and its tools for meeting regulatory rules, the Journal reported. The platform is aiming for a fourth-quarter launch, but it still needs regulators’ approval.

ICE has also signed up Securitize to issue tokenized shares for companies and funds, under a deal announced this year.

The NYSE deal would be a big step up. We pulled the latest network breakdown from rwa.xyz, which tracks tokenized shares that investors can hold in their own wallets.

The market itself is still small next to the stock market. All the tokens it tracks add up to $3.73 billion, held by about 4.8 million wallet addresses.

The NYSE could change that scale. Every share settled through its platform would move on Avalanche, which no other chain can claim today.

There is a catch. Companies can refuse to have their shares tokenized. On OKXICE, a separate venue from OKX and ICE, 33 of the 62 companies first named had objected by late October.

On the daily chart, AVAX is just below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that weight recent prices more. The 50-day and 200-day EMAs both sit at about $9.05, so one level now does the work of two.

This comes after Keplr, a multichain wallet supporting Cosmos, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Starknet, stated it had received reports of unauthorized transactions on some Keplr accounts created with Google or Apple login.

The wallet provider stated that the incident has been escalated to the Web3Auth team, with both working together to investigate the matter.

Before Keplr's disclosure, Web3 wallet infrastructure provider Web3Auth said it was aware of a security issue affecting Web3Auth's services used by some third parties. It stated that it had temporarily paused the embedded wallet service in response to the issue; however, after an initial investigation, no evidence was found that MetaMask users were impacted.

In his X post, Mishaboar criticized social signing. "Social signing, the feature you may want to add to your wallet if you hate your users," Mishaboar wrote.

Social signing, the feature you may want to add to your wallet if you hate your users. The worst part is that the users that use the social signing option -and which will end up being hacked through it - are also often newbies, entering crypto for the first time. And the risk goes beyond the funds in your wallet - data leaks could link your real life identity to your holdings, which can have terrible consequences.

The concern is particularly significant for inexperienced crypto users who may not recognize the risks associated with connecting their personal accounts to wallet services. The most immediate and damaging development is the unfolding scandal itself. In early November 2026, Jensen Huang publicly admitted to an extramarital affair and apologized to his family and employees, while NVIDIA’s board launched an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation.

Shares already reacted with sharp volatility, including a roughly -9% single-day drop around the initial reporting. Beyond the personal drama, the episode has intensified scrutiny of NVIDIA’s China exposure and export-control compliance at a time when U.S.-China tech tensions remain elevated.

Additional pressure points include recent broad market weakness in high-valuation tech names, signs of digestion in AI infrastructure spending after years of explosive growth, and the simple reality that NVIDIA’s valuation still prices in near-perfect execution. Any confirmation of deeper security concerns or leadership disruption could accelerate institutional selling.

NVIDIA has already broken down from its recent highs near the $240 area and is trading around $186–$187, having sliced through multiple short-term support levels.

The stock has formed a clear lower-high, lower-low sequence on the daily and weekly charts, with elevated volume on down days signaling distribution.

The 50-day and 200-day moving averages are rolling over, and momentum indicators such as RSI have spent time in oversold territory without producing a sustained bounce—often a sign that sellers remain in control.

A decisive break below the $180–$175 zone would open the door to a measured-move decline targeting the mid-$100s, with further downside possible if the $150 psychological level fails.

In a full-panic scenario driven by a leadership crisis and regulatory shock, multi-year Fibonacci retracements and prior consolidation bases from earlier in the AI cycle could come into play, supporting a much deeper correction.

While NVIDIA remains a dominant force in accelerated computing, an escalating personal and national security scandal, potential leadership upheaval, and a market already questioning AI valuations create a plausible path to severe downside.

By January 1, 2027, in this highly unlikely but catastrophic scenario, NVIDIA stock could fall to the $55–$75 range, with a stretch downside target near $40 if confidence fully unravels.

While NVDA is unlikely to go this low, the Jensen Huang affair with a suspected Chinese spy hasn’t been fully unraveled, and further revelations could spell disaster for Nvidia.
