#5309. Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path shows how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, says user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction shows a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale says its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

The two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

This looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem shows pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

#5308. South Korean Exchanges May Now Store 99% of Customer Assets in Cold Wallets Post $6.3B Binance Hack

South Korea’s financial regulator is weighing stricter custody rules for cryptocurrency exchanges after the record $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to reports of an emergency meeting held this week.

The Financial Services Commission convened major domestic platforms, the Financial Supervisory Service and industry groups on November 2nd to review security practices after unauthorized withdrawals from Binance hot wallets. They urged exchanges to raise the proportion of customer assets kept in cold storage, offline and disconnected from the internet, alongside tighter access controls, continuous monitoring of deposits and withdrawals, and stronger incident-response measures.

Under existing rules in the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, exchanges must already hold at least 80% of user assets in cold wallets, yet discussions at the meeting explored pushing that threshold significantly higher, with some reports indicating consideration of a level around 99%. Major platforms already operate at different ratios, as Upbit has reported more than 99% offline, while others range from the mid-80s to mid-90s.

No final rule change has been announced, and the FSC’s public statements emphasize the need for greater offline holdings to limit exposure in the event of a breach without specifying a new mandatory percentage.

Higher cold-wallet requirements could reduce the liquid assets available for immediate withdrawals, potentially affecting smaller exchanges more than larger ones that already maintain elevated offline ratios, reflecting heightened regulatory focus on exchange security following the largest crypto theft on record, which investigators have linked to a North Korean hacking group.

The new development follows hackers draining roughly $6.3 billion from Binance hot wallets across 10 blockchains in about 20 minutes on October 29th, 2026, marking the largest crypto theft on record. Investigators link the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, which compromised the exchange’s transaction-signing systems. About half the funds were frozen by stablecoin issuers. Binance has since pledged to cover all losses from its reserves and company funds.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

#5306. Ripple's Schwartz Speaks Out About His Influence Over XRP Price

David Schwartz, former chief technology officer of Ripple and one of the original XRP Ledger architects, has responded to claims that he is partially to blame for XRP's poor performance.

In a recent interaction on the X social media platform, David Schwartz was challenged about his possible impact on the price of the Ripple-linked cryptocurrency.

"Don't run from this. You can honestly say you don't have anything to do with it? It's not unfounded anger," the user wrote.

Although David Schwartz does not entirely deny that he can have an impact on the price of XRP, he is clear that it is minimal.

"Can I honestly say that I have nothing to do with the price of XRP? I guess probably not nothing. But very little," David Schwartz responded.

The response from Schwartz comes in the wake of mounting anger within the XRP community about the token's long-running price slump.

Indeed, XRP has seen roughly a 50% decline in value over the past year, per data from CoinMarketCap. During this period, the token has seen several temporary spikes, but the overall trend has been downward.

Of course, XRP is not the only token experiencing such a dramatic drop in value.

Stellar (XLM), another prominent cryptocurrency that seeks to enable payments, has seen a very similar price trend over the same time period.

The interaction came on the back of a long post in which Schwartz lamented the rise in hostile replies he receives on X.

Schwartz, a Ripple veteran, disclosed that some users are actually following him into other discussions and then proceeding to either label him a fraud or criticize him for his work on XRP.

The Ripple veteran noted that he has now made the decision to block such users, as irrelevant crypto-related posts are disrupting his discussions with other users.

Nonetheless, he stressed that the decision affects both critics and fans. Even if someone makes a positive comment about XRP but in an unsuitable place, they might also get blocked.

He also emphasized that he has no issue with honest criticism or accusations that make sense and come with good arguments.

He is mostly annoyed with users who keep hijacking unrelated discussions to vent their frustration.

In fact, Schwartz even offered to unblock users who commit to not doing so in the future.

Schwartz stepped away from his day-to-day duties at Ripple at the end of 2025. He had worked at the firm for over a decade. However, he has not completely left Ripple.

Earlier this month, Schwartz clarified that he's still on Ripple's board of directors and holds the honorary title of CTO Emeritus.

Furthermore, he disclosed that he still meets with his old team twice a month.

#5305. Bitcoin vs Gold: History Points to a Potential BTC Comeback in 2027

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. As of Tuesday, November 10, the Bitcoin vs gold race has an unusual score for 2026: both are losing. Bitcoin (BTC) is down 15.1% this year, and gold is down 5.9%.

That is rare. We compared the two assets’ returns up to November 10 in every year since 2015. Both were down at this point only twice before, in 2018 and 2022.

Gold is still ahead on the year. Gold futures trade at $4,086 an ounce, 23% below their record close of $5,318 on January 29. Bitcoin, at $74,259, is 40.5% below its record close of $124,753 from October 2025.

The calendar favors gold too. In each of the past 11 years, whichever asset led on November 10 also finished the year ahead.

But 2018 and 2022 ended the same way: Bitcoin hit its cycle low within six weeks and then beat gold by a wide margin the next year. So is 2026 setting up the same turn for 2027?

The two earlier cases point the same way, though two cases are a small sample to build on.

Both rebounds came in the year before a Bitcoin halving, the event every four years that cuts the number of new coins miners receive by half. The halvings fell in 2020 and 2024, and the next one is expected in 2028. That puts 2027 in the same slot as 2019 and 2023.

This year itself looks settled. Bitcoin beat gold in 8 of the 11 full years since 2015, and gold won only in 2018, 2022 and 2025. In every one of those 11 years, the asset that led on November 10 stayed ahead to December 31. Gold leads by about nine percentage points, so history hands it 2026, its second win in a row.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

Gold’s slide has been steep for a metal. It closed at a record $5,318 on January 29, fell as low as $3,899 on October 30, and now trades at $4,086.

Investors have not walked away. Gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold physical gold and trade like stocks. Worldwide, they added $2.7 billion in October, their fourth straight month of inflows, the World Gold Council reported on November 5. Their holdings rose 19 tonnes to a record 4,275 tonnes. Over the first ten months of the year, the funds took in $41 billion, the third-strongest run on record. North American funds were the exception, with small outflows.

Bitcoin has done better since February. Measured in gold, one Bitcoin bought 21.1 ounces on January 5. By February 23, that had fallen to 12.4 ounces, the lowest since March 2023. It now buys 18.2 ounces.

The gap since that February low is wide. Bitcoin is up 14.9% since February 23, while gold is down 21.8%. Since June 30, Bitcoin has gained 26.8% and gold 1.2%.

Discover: Bitcoin Miner and Whale Signals Spike on Binance: CryptoQuant Lays Out a Three-Part Test for a New Rally, and BTC Has Passed One

Both assets face the same test today. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes October’s consumer price index (CPI), the main measure of inflation, at 8:30 a.m. in New York, or 13:30 UTC.

Bitcoin trades at $74,278 ahead of the release. On Sunday, it fell to $73,510, its lowest price since August 21.

On the daily chart, where each candle covers one day, Bitcoin sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 200-day EMA stands at $76,480 and the 50-day EMA at $79,124.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

For gold, the line to watch is $3,899, the October 30 low. In the Bitcoin vs gold race, gold is on track to take 2026. If Bitcoin holds $73,510 and its 2018 and 2022 pattern repeats, 2027 is the year history gives to Bitcoin.

#5304. Binance's CZ Calls for Crypto Industry Unity

Former Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ) is pleading for more unity in the cryptocurrency space, claiming that bickering between different crypto factions doesn't make much sense as digital assets are tightly connected.

"Most crypto assets go up and down together. % might vary a bit, but what's happening to one affects everyone. In-fighting in this space makes zero sense," CZ tweeted.

He capped the post with a simple message pleading for unity: "We need to be: decentralized but united."

CZ was reacting to a social media post that pointed out how crises involving exchanges in the past had affected their respective tokens' prices.

The post pointed to the FTX fiasco in 2022, the WazirX hack in 2024, and the recent security breach at Bitget as examples of how troubles at exchanges can result in significant market losses.

The discussion even pointed to the massive hack at Binance on Oct. 29, which makes CZ's plea for more unity across the crypto space all the more relevant.

The crypto space is currently grappling with one of the biggest security breaches in recent memory.

Binance suffered a staggering $6.34 billion hack on Oct. 29 after hackers broke into the exchange's internal wallet signing infrastructure.

Several digital assets, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, and Solana, were all impacted by the hack.

Binance has assured users that it will bear the losses from the hack, as opposed to passing them along to customers. According to the exchange's update shared on Nov. 3, around $2.85 billion in stolen funds have been frozen or intercepted, while 98% of affected token assets have been replenished.

In recent days, CZ has been quite vocal about cybersecurity threats.

On Nov. 5, he advised crypto traders to revoke API keys for the third-party trading platform SignalPlus after it was reported that there might have been a security breach.

Meanwhile, CZ also warned his followers against fake websites posing as Trust Wallet, stressing that people shouldn't mistake domains ending in ".cam" for legitimate ".com" ones.

Furthermore, he asked iPhone users to ensure that their OS is up to date following reports of vulnerabilities that could leave crypto holders susceptible to malicious attacks.

#5303. Roger Ver Buying Bitcoin Cash Again? Suspicious $163,000 Swap Raises Eyebrows

A mysterious $163,000 crypto transaction has fueled rumors that Roger Ver, the controversial Bitcoin evangelist also known as 'Bitcoin Jesus,' may be purchasing Bitcoin Cash (BCH) once more.

According to on-chain analytics platform Onchain Lens, 73.31 Ethereum (ETH) coins were recently swapped for around 655.74 BCH coins (around $163,000) with the help of the decentralized cross-chain protocol THORChain.

Ver was famously an avid proponent of BCH, hailing it as a better option than the original Bitcoin network.

However, Onchain Lens didn't offer definitive proof that the wallet in question belongs to Ver.

Ver, a crypto pioneer who first entered the crypto space in 2011, quickly rose to become one of the most recognizable early Bitcoin advocates.

He was so passionate about the digital asset that he even earned the moniker 'Bitcoin Jesus' for his aggressive promotion of the cryptocurrency.

But as Bitcoin's controversial scaling debate (which ultimately saw the birth of Bitcoin Cash in August 2017) kicked off, Ver's relations with Bitcoin's mainstream community took a hit.

Ver quickly emerged as one of Bitcoin Cash's most vocal champions.

He passionately argued that BCH's larger block sizes and lower fees help keep Bitcoin true to its roots as a peer-to-peer electronic cash system.

For the past year, Roger Ver has been in the news mostly due to his well-publicized legal dispute with the U.S. government.

Back in April 2024, the crypto entrepreneur was arrested in Spain after U.S. authorities accused him of failing to pay roughly $48M in taxes on his massive Bitcoin holdings and transactions.

Ver, who renounced his U.S. citizenship back in 2014, insisted the prosecution was unjust.

He persistently tried to poke holes in the government's argument.

In June 2025, Ver upped the ante even further.

He took Spain to the European Court of Human Rights to contest the country's decision to extradite him to the U.S.

But the feud took a bombshell twist in October 2025.

Ver and the U.S. Justice Department reached a settlement through a deferred prosecution agreement.

The cryptocurrency figure agreed to pay almost $50 million in unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest.

NVIDIA tokenized stocks traded through a shock on Sunday, November 8, when news about Nvidia’s CEO broke while Wall Street was closed. At 20:12 UTC, CNBC reported that Nvidia’s board was investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China.

The stock market was closed. Tokenized versions of Nvidia, which trade around the clock on crypto platforms, were not. Within 30 minutes, Nvidia’s market on Hyperliquid fell 3.3%.

By the time Wall Street opened on Monday, 18 hours later, the token traders had already found the price. Hyperliquid’s Nvidia market stood at $173.27 a minute before the opening bell. Nvidia opened at $173.07, just 0.1% away.

Nvidia reports earnings on November 17, after the market closes. So can tokenized stocks call the move again?

The weekend gave tokenized markets a clean test. Nvidia closed Friday at $186.64 on the Nasdaq, and nothing traded on Wall Street until pre-market trading opened at 4 a.m. in New York on Monday, or 09:00 UTC.

We tracked Nvidia’s price on Hyperliquid minute by minute. The market there is a perpetual contract run by trade.xyz, a type of futures contract with no expiry date that follows the share price.

Backed tokens moved the same way. NVIDIA xStock (NVDAx), a token on Solana backed by real Nvidia shares, fell from $188.13 on Sunday at 20:00 UTC to $175.98 by 08:00 UTC on Monday. Hourly prices on CoinGecko show the same overnight slide.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

The news pulled in traders. Between Friday’s close and Monday’s pre-market, $258.5 million worth of Nvidia traded on Hyperliquid.

That is 4.7 times the average of the four weekends before, when the same 60-hour window saw $33 million to $72 million.

The timing explains it. Over a normal weekend, almost nothing happens to Nvidia, so the tokenized market is quiet. This weekend, it was one of the few places where traders could act on the news for about 13 hours.

There is an irony here. On November 2, Nvidia joined the companies objecting to tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, the planned venue from NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and the crypto exchange OKX.

The next big Nvidia news will also land when Wall Street is mostly closed. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 17, after the market closes, with a call at 5 p.m. in New York.

The regular after-hours session runs until 8 p.m. in New York. From then until 4 a.m., tokenized markets are among the few places still trading Nvidia.

The test will be harder this time. Weekend news hit a quiet market with one clear direction. Earnings bring a flood of numbers at once, and the first move after a report often reverses.

Nvidia trades at $173.17 on the Nasdaq on Tuesday, down 3.1% after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data. It touched $170.12, its lowest price since March 31. It is 28% below its record close of $239.24 on October 6.

On Hyperliquid’s four-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, Nvidia sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 50-period EMA stands at $189.53 and the 200-period EMA at $206.78.

#5301. Web3Auth Exploit Doesn't Affect Trust Wallet: Products That Might be Affected

Crypto industry is dealing with another security turmoil, as a breach at Web3Auth, the wallet authentication infrastructure owned by Consensys, has exposed private keys of certain Keplr wallets, according to the official statement of TrustWallet representative on X.

The November 7 incident led to emergency service suspensions and recovery efforts, which could add pressure to an already fragile crypto market.

Web3Auth confirmed that a security issue in its infrastructure had compromised certain embedded wallets integrated with Keplr, especially accounts created through Google or Apple login.

Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery estimates that attackers drained at least $6 million from more than 44,000 wallets.

Those wallets sit across eight Cosmos ecosystem networks, including Cosmos Hub, Osmosis, Celestia and Injective.

Keplr warned users from depositing into compromised accounts and Web3Auth on their side suspended embedded wallet service, actively working on a recovery of vulnerable assets.

MetaMask stated that there is no evidence of affected users, though the situation is still under control. Trust Wallet has been unaffected, says its representative Felix. The impact on other third-party integrations is yet to be confirmed.

On October 29, Binance reportedly suffered a massive security breach involving around $6.3 billion, while Bitget was hit by an exploit estimated at $387.5 million in September.

Earlier in 2026, KelpDAO lost around $290 million after an exploit involving cross-chain infrastructure.

DeFi protocols, wallet infrastructures, smart contracts: those kinds of incidents are relevant for almost every project on the market. Exploits directly affect market sentiment, investors losses and safety in the industry in general.

Projects that rely on embedded wallet technology and Cosmos-related assets have unfortunately been affected directly and repeated security failures might damage their market picture state even further.

Luckily, there's no proven link between the Web3Auth expoit and declines on the market as a whole, including assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum. The investigations and rapid protocol patches are being released after more than 24 hours since the discovery.

#5300. Cardano goes on-chain with criminal evidence tracking for police in India’s most populous state

Cardano (ADA) is expanding its real-world utility after police in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, began using the blockchain to track forensic evidence in active criminal cases.

The Cardano Foundation announced the deployment on Monday, revealing that every evidence scan and laboratory result is stored on-chain to strengthen record integrity during investigations.

Notably, TrivolveTech developed the Forensic Management System (FMS) in collaboration with Quixy. The project uses Cardano as an underlying verification layer, allowing police personnel to continue working through a conventional application without directly interacting with blockchain infrastructure.

The system addresses a potential weakness in conventional forensic procedures, where a shared case number can expose evidence to interference as it moves between police officers and separate laboratories. TrivolveTech designed FMS to replace that common identifier with unique codes for individual evidence handlers, limiting the ability to link records across different stages of an investigation.

Moreover, evidence boxes carry secure QR codes that can only be read through the FMS application. Each scan creates a record associated with the responsible handler, while cryptographic hashes are anchored to Cardano. These hashes function as digital fingerprints, allowing investigators to identify changes to recorded information during subsequent verification.

“Police evidence handling depends on trust between departments that are deliberately kept separate,” TrivolveTech founder and CEO Rahul Konudula said. “Each handler now works from an identifier meaningful only to their own step, and every scan becomes a permanent record on Cardano,” he added.

However, the system cannot confirm that evidence was collected properly or prevent physical tampering. Its value lies in the attributable digital trail it creates, which can show how evidence was handled and whether its records have been changed.

The Uttar Pradesh deployment adds to Cardano’s growing list of applications beyond cryptocurrency transactions. Last Wednesday, the Cardano Foundation reported that more than 100,000 farms in India had been registered on the blockchain through an agricultural initiative associated with the Syngenta Foundation. The project aims to make agricultural records more verifiable and reusable across lending, insurance, and government services.

Cardano is also pursuing education initiatives. The next day, the foundation announced that Cardano Academy would contribute a session on Cardano fundamentals and its extended unspent transaction output model to the University of Nicosia’s online Blockchain and Digital Assets course.

That said, Cardano is not the only blockchain network being used to secure official records. In Kenya, the Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) recently launched a blockchain-based credential verification system using Avalanche, with more than 30 million academic records reported to have been moved onto the network.

The initiative aims to help employers, universities, and other institutions verify academic credentials while making fraudulent certificates easier to identify.

#5298. Telegram Doesn’t Need to Convert Crypto Users: 1M Wallets in 48 Hours Reveal Its Massive Distribution Advantage

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Telegram is gaining crypto users without having to convince them to download another app. More than 1 million self-custodial wallets appeared on the messaging platform within 48 hours. Founder Pavel Durov says the growth reflects a simple feature: wallets activate automatically when users receive Grams. The milestone shows Telegram’s biggest advantage in crypto: distribution.

Unlike traditional crypto wallets, Telegram’s native wallet operates inside an application millions already use daily. Crypto traders, project founders, airdrop hunters, and blockchain communities have long relied on Telegram. That existing audience gives its wallet a distribution advantage that standalone crypto applications must spend years building.

The latest growth also raises an interesting question about blockchain adoption. Does crypto really need another wave of new users, or does it need easier access for people already participating? Telegram could provide exactly that bridge, provided wallet registrations translate into meaningful economic activity.

Durov reported more than 1million new self-custodial wallets over 48 hours in an X post. The dashboard accompanying his announcement showed more than 1 million registrations across the period.

1M+ self-custodial Gram wallets activated on Telegram in just 48 hours. $GRAM is up 10% in 24h, the #1 gainer in the CMC top 100. pic.twitter.com/VGVTT5AZQk

According to Durov, users do not need to manually create a wallet before receiving crypto. Their wallets activate when someone sends them Grams.

This creates a potentially powerful viral distribution mechanism. One user sends tokens to another, introducing the recipient to an on-chain wallet. The recipient can then hold or transfer assets without leaving Telegram.

This approach removes several familiar barriers to crypto adoption. New users do not necessarily need to understand seed phrases, download separate applications, or navigate an exchange. Telegram already provides the social environment where these transactions can begin.

The platform also has more than one billion monthly users, giving its crypto ambitions an enormous potential audience. Even a small conversion rate could produce substantial wallet growth.

The latest wallet milestone is not the only sign of expanding activity across The Open Network (TON), the blockchain powering Telegram’s wallet. TON averaged 4.06 million daily transactions during October. The network also added approximately 2.73 million wallets throughout the month, its strongest monthly addition since October 2024.

Stablecoin activity offers another indication of growing utility. TON averaged 37,693 daily stablecoin users in October, representing a 23.44% increase from September.

The stablecoin figures are particularly interesting because they point toward activity beyond token speculation. Payments and transfers could give Telegram crypto a more practical role in everyday digital interactions.

TON’s stablecoin supply stood at $585 million today. Its decentralized finance total value locked, however, remained comparatively modest at approximately $44 million.

Payments, stablecoin transfers, digital collectibles, and Telegram’s mini-app ecosystem could provide reasons to return. These services could gradually make blockchain transactions feel like another ordinary messaging feature.

#5297. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

FinCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange says it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

#5295. Ripple's XRP Ledger Lending to Receive Repayment Fix

The XRP Ledger's lending protocol is in for a tidy-up of how loan repayments get rounded. In plain terms, the balance after each payment would match the schedule, the update has been discribed in the official Github pull request.

After an overpayment, TotalValueOutstanding is reset to the scheduled value of the new PeriodicPayment.

Under the LendingProtocolV1_2 amendment, each on-time LoanPay would bring TotalValueOutstanding down to the scheduled value with one payment fewer, capped at the rounded PeriodicPayment.

The first commit moves the scheduled-value calculation out of computeLoanProperties into a separate scheduledValue function, with no behavior change.

That way, LoanSet and LoanPay round it the same way. Zero-interest loans also need a floor on the principal part, because their value is rounded to nearest while the principal is rounded up. Tests run on Legacy, CashBasis and FixedPrecision vaults, with and without the amendment.

Today, each payment's value part is calculated on its own, so rounding can build up across payments. The last payment can then need one unit more than the rounded PeriodicPayment, and the value parts can alternate between payments.

With the change, a method called telescoping makes the value part of every on-time payment either the floor or the ceiling of PeriodicPayment, and at least one unit. The last payment becomes exactly the rounded PeriodicPayment.

There's little to no effect for users and investors today. The extra unit on the final payment changes little. Older loans that already carried one unit above their schedule simply keep it, so the last payment still needs the PeriodicPayment and a single unit, unless the borrower overpays first.

Small overpayments are mostly ignored; the transaction goes through successfully and charges no extra XRP whatsoever.

Activation date is yet to be determined: 80% of validators agreement is needed for two weeks in a row for the amendment to go through. No public vote for LendingProtocolV1_2 has been announced yet, so the timeline remains uncertain.

#5291. Forget ‘Ultrasound Money’? Vitalik Buterin Pushes New Ethereum Store-of-Value Vision

Ethereum co-creator Vitalik Buterin is challenging one of Ether’s most celebrated investment narratives, suggesting that the second-largest crypto’s long-term value should depend less on how many tokens the network burns and more on its ability to become a reliable store of value.

The remarks could signal a major shift in how Ethereum’s value proposition is presented, particularly as declining transaction-fee burns weaken the deflationary narrative that once made ETH attractive to investors.

In a Sunday morning post on X, Buterin outlined three main reasons for shifting attention away from Ethereum’s fee-burning narrative and toward its potential as a store of value.

First, he argued that ETH’s deflationary appeal was never as powerful as it seemed. Although the 2021 EIP-1559 upgrade introduced a mechanism to burn a portion of transaction fees, the amount of ETH destroyed has not always been enough to offset new token issuance. In his view, making fee burns the central measure of Ethereum’s success places too much emphasis on a single aspect of its token economics. According to Buterin, even if fee burns remain below 10% of the level required to offset new issuance indefinitely, Buterin said, “we should not feel sad,” adding that “the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.”

Another concern is that prioritizing ETH as a fee-burning asset could push Ethereum toward decisions that undermine its core principles. Buterin suggested that designing the network primarily to maximize transaction-fee burns could create tensions with decentralization and censorship resistance. Such an approach could require trade-offs that make the network less open and less resistant to external control, potentially weakening the very qualities that distinguish Ethereum from competing blockchain networks.

Notably, the fee-burning mechanism was central to Ethereum’s popular “ultrasound money” narrative, which gained significant traction among ETH investors during the 2021 bull run. The thesis suggested that by permanently removing a portion of transaction fees from circulation, Ethereum could become increasingly deflationary, potentially making ETH scarcer and more valuable over time.

He also sees an opportunity in the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence. As AI continues to disrupt industries and reshape economic activity, dependable financial infrastructure could become more valuable. “In the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued,” he wrote.

Buterin believes Ethereum’s emphasis on stability could give ETH a stronger store-of-value proposition in this changing environment, shifting the investment narrative away from token burns and toward the network’s ability to preserve trust over the long term.

Interestingly, Buterin’s position also found support from Solana co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko, who appeared to share his skepticism about making transaction fees the centerpiece of a blockchain’s value proposition. Yakovenko dismissed the idea of treating fees as the product, calling it “absolutely meaningless.” He argued that blockchain networks should focus on delivering tangible value to users rather than trying to control how much people pay to have their transactions included in a block.

#5288. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

Binance, world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, officially reopened Hyperliquid and Aptos withdrawals, giving users a freeway to operate with HYPE and APT tokens. Confirmed by Yi He, platform's co-founder and president, the resurrection of operation came after finalization of the audit. What lies behind the announcement is the conclusion of week-long retaliation with the HYPE community as holders of native Hyperliquid token needed to wait longer than others to be able to withdraw from Binance.

💁🏻‍♀️ Withdrawals have now been re-enabled for the following networks and assets: New: ✅ HYPE ✅ APT

The predecessor of this story is the biggest cyberattack in history when, according to the FBI and Chainalysis, the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor emptied Binance's hot wallets for about $6.3 billion in a matter of 20 minutes. What happened next is the exchange blocking $3 billion with the help of Tether, Circle; its pledge to cover 100% of users' money from the SAFU fund; and thorough audits across Solana and Ethereum chains. Then, starting November 1, Binance started reopening tokens for withdrawal.

HYPE was the last to become eligible and the community behind DeFi giant met such a measure with discontent, crying about sabotage and unfair competition tactics. It's not that deep: Hyperliquid, being the headliner of decentralized finance, amasses a big share of the pie in on-chain derivatives trading, and of course this affects Binance's business.

The retaliation between the two has continued since 2025 when Hyperliquid founder Jeff Yan publicly accused Binance of lowering liquidations data after the October 10, 2025 event, when positions worth around $40 billion were marginally closed across the crypto market. Binance then delayed the spot listing of HYPE token until September 24, 2026 and gave it 'Seed Tag', which is usually applied to high-risk cryptocurrencies. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao diplomatically refused the accusations and said that strong decentralized exchanges on the contrary increase 'the pie' for the whole industry.

The delay indeed has a technical aspect. HYPE operates within its own Layer-1, HyperEVM. Auditing a custom blockchain architecture — not standard EVM or Solana-based — in the aftermath of such a hack requires more time and attention to be carried out properly.

In the wake of the cybersecurity crisis the pause was still interpreted as corporate vengeance. This makes Yi He's words and the demonstrative relaunch of withdrawals a sign that obligations for clients take priority over market rivalry.

Bitcoin’s cycle bottom is likely already in or very close, as a Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Bitcoin bottom prediction highlights a final low expected in the $60,000–$68,000 zone by late December 2026 or early January 2027 at the latest. As of November 11, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $73,700–$73,900, roughly 41% below its October 2025 all-time high around $126,000.

The market has been grinding lower after a failed recovery attempt into the low $80,000s, with recent sessions testing the psychologically important $73,000 level. While the short-term trend remains soft, longer-term structure and historical cycle patterns suggest the deepest part of the correction is largely complete.

Bitcoin is consolidating in a tight range after a multi-week decline. Immediate support sits at the $73,000 round number, which coincides with recent daily lows, the approximate 200-day moving average, and prior structural levels from earlier in the year.

A daily close below $73,000 would open the door to the next support cluster near $71,500 (prior swing area) and then the 50-day moving average zone around $68,500. Deeper support resides in the $62,000–$65,000 region, with the July 2026 low near $57,700–$58,000 acting as the major cycle floor.

On the upside, resistance is layered at $75,000, followed by the more significant $80,000 area. Momentum indicators such as the RSI have cooled into neutral-to-oversold territory on daily timeframes, leaving room for either a relief bounce or one final liquidity sweep lower before a more durable base forms.

Volume has been elevated on down days, consistent with distribution by short-term holders, but longer-term holder metrics and the 200-week moving average (historically a strong demand zone) continue to provide a structural floor.

Bitcoin | Net shorts just hit an ATH.The last 4 times we saw these levels, they marked a major bottom. pic.twitter.com/n9DkeYEYqy

My base-case view is that the primary cycle low was printed in July 2026 near $58,000. That level marked a roughly 54% drawdown from the prior peak, shallower than the 70–80%+ declines of previous bear markets, reflecting Bitcoin’s growing institutional base and ETF demand.

The current pullback into the low $70,000s looks more like a higher-low retest or secondary correction within a broader bottoming process rather than the start of a new leg down. If $73,000 fails, a final flush into the $62,000–$68,000 zone remains the most probable destination.

This area aligns with Fibonacci retracements of the 2025–2026 rally, prior demand zones, and the upper end of the July low region. I expect any such move to occur relatively quickly, within the next four to eight weeks, driven by residual profit-taking, macro uncertainty, or year-end positioning.

By late December 2026 or the first half of January 2027 at the latest, this process should be complete. A sustained defense of the $68,000–$70,000 area (or a higher low above $70,000) would strongly support the thesis that the bottom is in.

Conversely, a decisive break below the July low near $58,000 would invalidate the constructive view and open a path toward $50,000–$55,000, though that outcome currently carries lower probability given the maturity of the correction and the strength of long-term holder support.

In short, Bitcoin appears to be in the late stages of its post-2025 correction. The most likely final low sits in the $60,000–$68,000 range, timed for the remainder of Q4 2026 into very early 2027. Once that floor is confirmed with a higher low and a reclaim of $80,000, the stage would be set for a more meaningful recovery phase.

A discussion regarding the throughput of major blockchains emerged after an X user, 'Minus Wells,' claimed that 1,500 TPS is not the future of finance, not even 5,000, adding that this is roughly Visa's average throughput on a normal day.

"1,500 TPS is not the future of finance, not even 5,000. Sorry, they lied to you for engagement. That's roughly Visa's average throughput on a normal day. Congrats on matching the legacy system," Wells wrote.

It's a process. 1) Not every transaction needs to be settled in seconds immediately. Payment channels or higher layers like Dassie (Interledger) are much better suited for mass (micro) payments. MasterCard is looking to do more hackathons afaik with the XRP Ledger after the successful one at Swell leveraging this and AI. Batched settlement of institutions is good enough in the meantime to be very beneficial vs tradFi. Until: 2) I strongly believe we'll scale the L1s very sharply, not only XRPL, thanks to AI helping us to advance this tech even further. We are continuously pushing throughput higher and there is a lot of potential (!!!) for significantly more.

While Visa's network (VisaNet) has a technical capacity of 65,000 to over 83,000 transactions per second (TPS), its actual average volume runs at approximately 8,100 to 8,500 TPS. The post attracted attention in the XRP community given that the XRP Ledger sustains a throughput of 1,500 transactions per second (1,500 TPS) on commodity hardware.

Wells clarified he was not personally attacking XRP, claiming that XRPL, Avalanche, Stellar, Tezos L1, Cardano's Leios experiments, and OP Mainnet swap tests have all published throughput figures or results below 5,000 TPS. "Those aren't equivalent tests or necessarily current hard ceilings. But the question applies to everyone: can the infrastructure handle the demand future finance could bring?" he asked.

Hussein Zangana (Vet), XRP Ledger Foundation director of community, responded to claims regarding L1 blockchains' scalability with respect to XRP, saying "it's a process."

Vet made a case for the comparatively lower TPS of decentralized blockchains, noting that not every transaction needs to be settled in seconds. He pointed out that payment channels or higher layers like Dassie (Interledger) are much better suited for mass (micro) payments.

With respect to XRP, Vet noted that Mastercard is looking to do more hackathons with the XRP Ledger after a successful one at the Swell event while leveraging AI.

Batch, which allows multiple transactions to be bundled into a batch that is processed all together and was launched on the XRPL mainnet in October 2026, stands to benefit the XRP Ledger in this regard. "Batched settlement of institutions is good enough in the meantime to be very beneficial vs. TradFi," Vet added.

The XRP Ledger Foundation director of community highlighted massive scaling potential for the XRP Ledger and L1 blockchains.

"I strongly believe we'll scale the L1s very sharply, not only XRPL, thanks to AI helping us to advance this tech even further. We are continuously pushing throughput higher and there is a lot of potential (!!!) for significantly more," Vet wrote.

Ripple's director of engineering Viijay Khanna directly confirmed that the company is readying 'big plans' for XRP Ledger in 2027. The remark came amid the debates around the blockchain's speed, when critics put the XRP network's stats (around 1,500 transactions per second) against the average daily load of Visa, labeling the XRPL "an outdated copy of legacy payment systems".

"We have big plans for performance improvements lined up for 2027", said Khanna, effectively ending speculations.

Ripple's engineering department is aiming to exit the race for beautiful numbers behind the TPS metric. The logic is that the basic Layer-1 does not need to digest millions of small transactions directly. Retail microtraffic then goes to the second layer like Dassie (Interledger). The task of the main layer thus becomes maintaining large funds of banks and institutions.

The first step to this kind of independence from "heavy blockchain metal" was made this month with the fresh release of xrpld 3.3.0 which cut the appetite of nodes to RAM by 13-23%.

Technical audits show that the issue was not in simple code flaws, but the caprices of the system's allocator: the software was literally withholding the server's resources after the cache emptying. Bug fix therefore allowed validators to radically decrease infrastructure costs.

For further improvement of the current operational environment on November 4, the network got a fixCleanup package.

Khanna's short commentary is not an attempt to snuff out critics, but a marker of an ecosystem's overhaul for the needs of commercial banks. Ripple's president Monica Long has already announced a plan to relay the big chunk of the company's clients' payments directly on XRP Ledger. Cross-border remittances will be tied to new lending infrastructure as well.

To make sure the network will not flood from institutional funds, XRP Ledger Foundation already presented a 2027 roadmap with these as main highlights:

The overhaul of XRP Ledger is a preventive hit on the network's future overload. Ripple ecosystem builders rewrite the basis, using AI teams for strict testing and code optimization. XRP Ledger is being readied for the moment when transactions with RLUSD stablecoin, tokenized stocks trading, and interbank lending become a routine and not just pilot projects.

#5283. Are Bitcoin Bears Priced In? Deutsche Bank’s Quiet Move Marks Major Counter-Signal For BTC USD

Deutsche Bank opened its digital asset custody service to institutional and corporate clients on Wednesday, November 11, starting with Bitcoin, Ether and three stablecoins. Germany’s largest bank now holds the private keys to clients’ coins itself, three years after it first applied for a German crypto custody licence.

The launch lands in a gloomy market. Bitcoin trades at $73,943, down 5.8% in a week. That is 41% below its October 2025 record of $126,080.

The crowd is gloomier still. Analytics firm Santiment counts more negative than positive social media comments on BTC, Ether and XRP. It reads that disbelief as a sign of a classic bullish counter signal, the idea that markets tend to turn when most traders expect them to fall.

We checked that idea against eight years of the Crypto Fear & Greed Index. It works, but only at the extremes.

The service does two things at the start. It stores clients’ coins and moves them on request, between the bank’s own warm and cold wallets or out to third parties. Trading is not part of it.

The bank’s custody site lists the details:

Clients reach it through Autobahn, the same platform they already use for the bank’s other services. That is the selling point for a corporate treasurer: no new crypto firm to vet, and no in-house wallet team to build.

The bank set out the plan in a September 16 release, with tokenized securities on its roadmap. “Digital assets are not a replacement for the traditional financial system but an important complement to it,” said Gerald Podobnik, co-head of Deutsche Bank’s Corporate Bank.

The same release warned that crypto held this way is not covered by a deposit guarantee like ordinary bank deposits.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

Santiment tracks the ratio of positive to negative comments about each coin on social media. A reading of 1 means the two are even, and anything below 1 means the crowd is more negative than positive.

On Tuesday, all three large coins sat below that line on its Sanbase charts, which track Santiment’s daily positive-to-negative ratio:

The firm called BTC and Ether sentiment “very bearish” and XRP “extremely bearish”. Its view is that crowds tend to be most bearish near a bottom, so heavy pessimism can mark a turn higher.

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index tells the same story. It reads 29 on Wednesday, in “fear”, down from 32 on Tuesday. It has read 29 or lower on 192 of the 315 days so far in 2026.

So does fear pay? We matched every daily reading of the Fear & Greed Index since February 2018 with Bitcoin’s daily close on Binance 30 days later. That gave 3,172 days to test.

The counter signal Santiment describes has worked in deep panic, not in ordinary gloom. Moderate fear has been the normal state of 2026, and it has not marked a bottom on its own.

The Fear & Greed reading would need to fall another 10 points or more to reach the zone where buying the fear has paid. By that test, the crowd is bearish, but not yet bearish enough.

Bitcoin trades at $73,943 on Binance. On Tuesday, it touched $72,727, its lowest price since August 21.

On the daily chart, where each candle covers one day, BTC sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 200-day EMA stands at $76,451 and the 50-day EMA at $78,906.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

Deutsche Bank’s custody desk is built for the long run, and it won’t move the price this week. For the counter signal, the history is clear: it has fired in deep fear, below 20, and the index sits at 29.

Dogecoin cofounder Billy Markus shared a lighthearted observation about Japan's unique dog culture in a post on X, pointing out the popularity of Shiba Inu dogs in Japan.

"Like, 50% of the dogs I see in Japan are Shiba Inu," wrote Markus, who goes by the online handle Shibetoshi Nakamoto.

like 50% of the dogs i see in japan are shiba inu i love japan

The Dogecoin cofounder's comment is based on his own observation when he was in Japan, where the Shiba Inu breed has deep cultural roots and is still one of the country's most recognizable native dog breeds. Markus' observation is noteworthy, as he is the cofounder of Dogecoin, a cryptocurrency that draws its origins from the Shiba Inu dog.

On December 6, 2013, Dogecoin was launched, taking influence from the famous Doge meme: an image of a very adorable Shiba Inu dog with multi-colored Comic Sans text that appears as the dog's "thought bubbles."

This famous meme was based on a 2010 photograph of a Japanese female Shiba Inu dog, Kabosu, adopted by Japanese kindergarten teacher Atsuko Satō from an animal shelter in 2008. This helped establish the dog-themed cryptocurrency trend that later inspired several other tokens, including Shiba Inu (SHIB).

Kabosu, a Japanese Shiba Inu, inspired a generation of online jokes and became the face of Dogecoin cryptocurrency. Kabosu was the face of the breezy Doge meme, her quizzical expression surrounded by an inner monologue of choppy phrases in bad grammar written in rainbow-colored Comic Sans font.

In 2010, two years after adopting Kabosu from a puppy mill where she would otherwise have been put down, Ms. Satō, a teacher from Sakura, east of Tokyo, took a picture of her pet crossing her paws on the sofa. She posted the image on her blog, from where it spread to online forum Reddit and became a meme that bounced from college bedrooms to office email chains.

This inspired Dogecoin, which was started as a joke by two software engineers, Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer, and is now the 12th largest cryptocurrency, with a market capitalization of $11.17 billion, according to CoinMarketCap data.

Kabosu, the dog behind the "doge" meme, died in May 2024 after 14 years of internet fame.

#5281. ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For users, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

As the Ethereum community debated the ability of the network to sustain on old power, Vitalik Buterin showed up with a manifesto which completely zeroes out all the panic around mainnet's decreasing revenue. The "red line" behind Vitalik's updated vision is that the community should stop being fixated on the idea of ETH as "fee-burninng token". For a basic blockchain layer worth $270 billion, attempts to build evaluation on the amount of gas burned are a dead end. For Vitalik, the novel of "ETH as store of value (SoV)" is much more viable amid all the global uncertainty around.

This U-turn, taken by a key visionary of the ecosystem, happened at $2,240 for ETH and may drastically change all the plans developed with a focus on Glamsterdam architecture. The hard fork was initially projected for the logic of blockspace surplus, not the deficit. Ecosystem builders are already readying expansion of L1 capacity with the help of EIP-8037 (tariffs calibration) and EIP-7928 (parallel production) with an aim to raise gas limits up to 200 million units. The logic is that the excess of free space will cheapen the transactions, while token burning rates will gradually be cut.

The market saw a risk of deflation in this concept. Vitalik took a front-step. By his estimates, the historical peaks of burning through EIP-1559 "never were as strong as they seemed". They were dependent on inner cyclical activity of crypto speculations. And it itself was falling once every bear market started.

EIP-1559 is not going anywhere, and Vitalik openly says "don't be sad" if the volume of gas burned will forever stay below the 10% mark. The source of value for Ethereum lies in completely another dimension.

Solana's co-founder, Anatoly Yakovenko, unexpectedly aligned with Buterin on this matter. "You can't focus on fees as the products", he said, calling such an idea "absolutely meaningless". According to Yakovenko, the blockchain network must generate real value for the end users, not control the price of getting into the block.

Vitalik is absolutely right that you can’t focus on fees as the product. That’s absolutely meaningless. You need to pick a product, the thing that brings value to people, and do that really well.

There is lots of technical stuff and philosophy around, but what the missed deadline on the testnet and Vitalik's manifesto reveal is that Ethereum opts for long-term, secure, and even a bit boring stability of the basic layer. Infra doesn't try to flirt with the market through deflationary records.

"And that's part of the reason we created Flare because we feel like there's always been more that can and should be done with XRP," the Flare CEO added.
