#5156. DeepMind’s AI humanoids are already doing factory work at Mercedes

DeepMind reports 96% success in a parts-sorting pilot on Mercedes-Benz production lines in Germany and Hungary. Human-intervention rates remain undisclosed.

Google DeepMind says robot maker Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoids achieved a 96% success rate sorting automotive parts on active Mercedes-Benz production lines, using AI to handle preparation work that feeds vehicle assembly.

The company disclosed the proof of concept on Nov. 10, identifying sites in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. The work provides a specific test for its Gemini Robotics 2.5 model: arranging the components needed by the people building cars.

The task was automotive kitting, which involves taking parts from bulk bins and organizing them in the order needed for each vehicle. DeepMind's example involved picking up metal brackets and placing them into sequencing containers. That ties the demonstration to a defined step in preparing an assembly line's supplies. The trays are meant to match the parts needed for each vehicle, so getting the sequence right is part of the task. The robot has to organize the components as well as move them.

Apollo 2 prepared parts in vehicle order in DeepMind's Mercedes-Benz proof of concept.

A defined preparation task is working in a pilot; the sustained operating burden remains unquantified.

Two models divided the work. Gemini Robotics ER tracked the workflow, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled the robot's hands and arms, according to DeepMind.

Apptronik CEO Jeff Cardenas said in the announcement that the models improved after a few weeks of post-training and transferred to Mercedes production with little performance drop-off.

The relationship predates this result. In March 2024, Apptronik announced an agreement to explore uses for its original Apollo, including delivering assembly kits, inspecting components and transporting containers of kitted parts. It argued that humanoids could handle repetitive, physically demanding work in spaces designed for people, potentially avoiding a full factory redesign.

DeepMind calls the kitting autonomous, but does not define whether success means an individual pick, a completed tray or another unit. Its disclosure provides no trial count and does not report reset frequency, human-intervention rates, cycle times, uptime or operating costs.

For factory operators, the unanswered questions are how much work the robots finish in a shift and how often a person must step in to keep production moving.

The appointment follows the launch of Phase’s Layer 1 blockchain mainnet and AI agent services, backed by $45 million in founder funding.

SAN FRANCISCO, November 11, 2026 — Phase, a technology company building the operating layer for the AI agent economy, today announced that Yana Prikhodchenko, former CEO of Cointelegraph, has joined the company as co-founder and CEO. She will lead strategy, global expansion and commercial development, working alongside founder Kirill Eves, as Phase scales its decentralized infrastructure for autonomous AI agents.

Prikhodchenko joins Phase after nearly five years at Cointelegraph, where she served as CEO, leading a global team of more than 200 people and transforming the company from a crypto news platform into a diversified group spanning media, marketing, research, acceleration and industry events. Before joining Cointelegraph, she spent more than a decade in senior leadership roles at major banking and insurance companies, including Allianz.

Phase is building the operating layer for the AI agent economy, giving AI agents everything they need to operate autonomously, from accessing the open web and orchestrating AI models to performing computing tasks and making payments. These services run on Phase’s Layer 1 blockchain, powered by a decentralized network of everyday devices whose owners earn rewards for validating transactions and contributing connectivity and computing power.

“AI agents are moving from answering questions to performing real tasks on our behalf, but the infrastructure they depend on was not built for autonomous systems. Phase is building an open, decentralized network that anyone can participate in. My focus is to bring this technology to developers and businesses worldwide and build the ecosystem needed to support the next generation of AI agents,” said Yana Prikhodchenko, co-founder and CEO of Phase.

“Yana brings extensive leadership experience across media, technology and financial services, along with the operational expertise and industry relationships needed to take Phase into its next stage of growth. As we bring our technology to market, she will lead the company’s commercial development and global expansion,” said Kirill Eves, founder of Phase.

Phase is a technology company building the operating layer for the AI agent economy, with four integrated services that give AI agents everything they need to operate autonomously, from accessing the open web and orchestrating AI models to performing computing tasks and making payments. The platform runs on its own Layer 1 blockchain, powered by a decentralized network of everyday devices. Phase has received $45 million in funding from its founder, Kirill Eves.

Phase Proxy enables AI agents acting on behalf of users to access websites that restrict automated traffic through mobile and residential internet connections. Phase Router intelligently directs requests across leading AI models to optimize quality, performance and cost. Phase Compute harnesses the processing power of devices across the network to run open-weight AI models, while on-chain settlement enables autonomous payments using stablecoins and PHASE, the network’s native token. Phase is building its own AI model to serve as the platform’s central intelligence, capable of advanced reasoning, solving complex tasks independently and orchestrating other AI models.

Unlike most blockchain networks that require dedicated servers or token staking, Phase allows anyone to become a validator simply by downloading the app, without specialized hardware or upfront investment. Its reputation-based consensus and randomized validator selection secure the network and prevent control from concentrating in the hands of a few powerful operators. Phase rewards device owners with PHASE tokens for validating blocks and contributing connectivity and computing power, enabling millions of people to help build the AI economy and share in the value it creates.

#5150. PNC lets businesses accept USDC without keeping the crypto

Eligible corporate clients can accept Ethereum USDC payments and receive dollars in their PNC accounts. The limited Coinbase-powered pilot keeps the banking relationship intact.

PNC's incoming stablecoin pilot gives businesses a way to accept USDC without keeping their receipts in crypto. Under the limited program announced Nov. 9, eligible Corporate & Institutional Banking clients receive USDC on Ethereum, with payments automatically converted 1-to-1 into dollars and deposited into a designated PNC account.

The payment travels over stablecoin infrastructure, but the receiving customer's balance ends up at the bank. That design keeps the deposit account in the payment relationship, even as the way of paying changes.

Coinbase supplies the underlying payment infrastructure through its Payment APIs, while PNC provides banking and treasury-management services.

The offering is a route for incoming USDC to become dollars in a banking relationship. It does not announce a PNC-issued stablecoin or put customer deposits on a blockchain.

Announced Nov. 9, 2026: PNC's limited pilot converts eligible corporate and institutional clients' incoming USDC into dollar deposits.

Dollar conversion alone does not reveal whether tokens are redeemed or transferred. The announcements do not identify either mechanism.

The disclosed PNC deposit endpoint is one part of the picture. Changes in payer and conversion balances, issuer bank deposits and reserve allocation determine the wider effect.

The customer's settlement destination is disclosed. Token supply and banking-system funding effects are separate questions.

Limited eligible-client pilot. Conversion counterparty, redemption versus inventory route, timing, fees, usage and measured deposit effects are undisclosed. Dashed paths illustrate unknown mechanisms or information needed for analysis, not verified PNC fund flows. Fed material is staff analysis, not PNC outcome data.

Qualitative route diagram from the November 9 provider announcements. Arrows in the main view show the announced customer sequence, not timing or volume. Selectable views distinguish unresolved token disposition from systemwide funding analysis. No calculations or quantitative charts.

Limited eligible-client pilot. Conversion counterparty, redemption versus inventory route, timing, fees, usage and measured deposit effects are undisclosed. Dashed paths illustrate unknown mechanisms or information needed for analysis, not verified PNC fund flows. Fed material is staff analysis, not PNC outcome data.

CryptoSlate's September coverage of the Coinbase and Moov banking partnership left institution-specific fiat settlement routes unresolved. PNC names the receiving account for its own pilot, answering a practical question for a corporate treasury: where do the proceeds arrive after someone pays in stablecoins?

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

For banks, that design fits an adaptation strategy described by Federal Reserve staff: respond to new payment competition through products, infrastructure and partnerships while continuing to serve customers. The pilot puts that approach into a specific receiving-payment service.

A credit in the receiving customer's PNC account tells us where that customer's money arrives. It does not tell us how the payer acquired USDC, who supplied the conversion dollars, or which other balances changed along the way. Those offsetting movements matter to whether the banking system gains funding overall.

A March 30 Federal Reserve staff model illustrates a possible inventory route. In its hypothetical cross-border payment, a recipient can sell stablecoins and deposit local currency while an intermediary retains the tokens. Fees and delays in exchanging tokens for currency can influence how much inventory intermediaries hold.

In a May 1 analysis of banks' responses to stablecoins, Fed staff distinguished aggregate deposit levels from their composition. Money can return to banks through issuers holding reserve deposits or through securities dealers redepositing proceeds. Stablecoin activity can shift the ownership and location of deposits without necessarily reducing the banking system's total deposits one-for-one.

The receiving customer's conversion is also separate from the issuer-side reserve choices discussed in CryptoSlate's October coverage.

For a business, the practical test is how efficiently those receipts become usable cash. PNC and Coinbase describe faster access to funds and greater cross-border efficiency as intended benefits. Their November announcements leave the precise settlement deadline, spendable-funds availability, operating hours, restrictions and pilot fees unspecified.

Those terms matter when comparing a blockchain transfer with the time it takes for the resulting bank balance to become available to spend. The companies have also disclosed no participating-client count, processed transaction volume or measured deposit effect in these announcements.

PNC has specified the customer's destination: a dollar deposit. The next evidence to watch is whether eligible businesses use the route and how it performs for their treasury operations.

#5146. Britain should ask crypto founders what would have kept them here

Britain counts the people it loses, but listening to crypto founders who leave could reveal what would persuade the next generation to stay.

When I asked Praneet Sinha why he left Britain, he said it came down to operational and financial efficiency. He co-founded his crypto startup, Moongate, in London in 2022. The business planned to collect its fees in crypto, which would mean converting that revenue into fiat to pay salaries and running costs.

“RAK DAO (Ras Al Khaimah Digital Assets Oasis) made more sense for us from a regulatory and business standpoint,” he told me. “It offered a more crypto-friendly environment and tax advantages, particularly around converting crypto revenue into fiat to fund our operating expenses.”

That is why he moved the business from the UK to the UAE, setting up in RAK DAO, a free zone for digital-asset companies in Ras Al Khaimah. He is now based in Abu Dhabi, having moved in August 2024. Moongate Labs Ltd, the UK company, was dissolved in July 2025, and MoonPay acquired the business in June 2026.

Borders constrain ambition less than at any point in living memory, and internet capital markets mean a founder can build from almost anywhere. Yet people are crossing them anyway.

Between 2021 and 2025, Britain lost a net 507,000 of its own nationals, based on ONS long-term migration data. The figure is the cumulative total of annual net losses over those five years, with a provisional 136,000 in 2025 alone.

The count starts in 2021 for a reason. In November 2025, the ONS changed how it counts British nationals, replacing a survey that had been underestimating British emigration. The revised figures only go back to 2021.

Those figures cover British nationals across all lines of work. They cannot tell us how many were crypto founders, whether their businesses left with them, or how much tax revenue the country lost.

We can estimate the scale of this loss, but can we say what the main cause of it is?

The ONS and the Migration Observatory concede the difficulty themselves, with the ONS admitting that it cannot carry out high-quality surveys overseas or access the administrative data foreign governments hold about their populations, and the Migration Observatory saying that “relatively little is known about which British citizens leave the UK, or the reasons why.”

The absence of hard data also explains the absence of urgency. No government has designated the exodus a national emergency, or a crisis for that matter.

Founders have been asked about this before. Tech Nation’s 2025 Growth Stage report surveyed them on why they would consider moving their headquarters out of the UK. At Superteam UK, we’re hearing more and more that our best founders want to leave for cities like Dubai, Singapore, New York and San Francisco. We wanted to hear from crypto founders who had already gone, so I started asking them directly.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

We mustn't settle for founders who are born or educated in the UK or who incorporate their businesses here, only to build their unicorns elsewhere. Here’s another reason by Arun Krishnakumar.

Krishnakumar has lived in Britain for nearly 21 years. He studied at the LSE and Oxford, worked at Barclays and PwC, and credits London’s “great schools generating great minds.” But when he chose an entrepreneurial career, he was constantly told that “if you were doing this in Silicon Valley, you would be in a much better place”. Citing American capital, culture and regulation, he plans to move to the US.

Capital has been heading in the same direction. In January 2025, a16z scaled back its UK presence to refocus on the US, less than two years after choosing London for its first office outside the US.

Stories like theirs tend to surface one at a time. Reasons why people leave the UK are largely anecdotal and often self-reported, either in the form of a LinkedIn post or an X talking head video.

The Brain Drain Wall, which I lead at Superteam UK, is our attempt to gather them in one place. Between 16 July and 21 October 2026, it received 576 submissions. Of those, 61 percent want to stay in Britain, 32 percent plan to leave, and 7 percent have already left. About 157 respondents, more than a quarter, are founders or C-suite executives. This group includes 63 people whose job title is founder, the most common designation on the Wall. Nearly half are based in London. All the responses were voluntary, so the Wall reflects people who chose to share their reasons with us.

Of the 226 who are leaving or have left, the most common reasons were quality of life (25.2 percent), the tax environment (24.3 percent), job opportunities (20.4 percent) and capital (12.4 percent). Together, tax and capital account for about 36.7 percent, more than quality of life alone.

Of the 350 staying, nearly half (48.9 percent) cited family and relationships, followed by career and opportunity (20.3 percent) and quality of life (12 percent).

We believe that, through network effects, if we can get enough people to share their main reasons for leaving the UK, it’ll give us a better understanding of which policy recommendations we can solidly present to the government instead of it just being a guessing game.

The goal is to find the causes behind the brain drain, then minimise or remove those barriers altogether. Hopefully, that will give people a compelling reason to stay in Britain.

Britain has spent years counting the people it loses. Now it’s time to ask them why. We’re asking because we want to know what would make them stay. So I put that question to Sinha: if the UK had matched what RAK DAO offered, would he have kept Moongate in London?

“Yes, it was another hassle to set up a company in a different country.”

Disclosure: Cessiah Lopez created and leads Superteam UK’s Brain Drain Wall project. This piece wasn’t written for the Brain Drain Wall bounties, wasn’t entered for a prize and wasn’t a paid placement.

#5144. Bitcoin Core Breaks Silence on Three Patched Security Vulnerabilities

Bitcoin Core developers have revealed three key security vulnerabilities, including a high-severity flaw that could potentially disrupt the mining capabilities of the Bitcoin network, preventing miners from creating new blocks.

As revealed in security advisories published on Nov. 10, the vulnerabilities impacted various elements of the Bitcoin Core software that powers many nodes underpinning the world's leading cryptocurrency.

One of the vulnerabilities, titled CVE-2025-62861, was rated as a high-severity issue due to its potential effect on Bitcoin miners.

The bug has the potential to create problems after a blockchain reorganization, which is when previously accepted blocks are replaced by the network with an alternative chain.

More precisely, the issue could cause an inconsistent state in the node's mempool, where all unconfirmed transactions are stored.

The vulnerability impacted Bitcoin Core software versions 28.0-28.2 and 29.0-29.1.

It was first reported on Sept. 26, 2025, by security researcher Niklas Goegge.

Beyond the mining vulnerability, Bitcoin Core developers have announced two further security problems, rated medium severity.

The first one (CVE-2025-62859) could enable malicious network participants to slow down Bitcoin block processing through an exploit that involves changes in transaction witness data.

Under some circumstances, it could make an affected node wait for up to 10 minutes before processing a block.

Moreover, such an attack could be repeated indefinitely on the node when the latter is running in specific configurations.

The vulnerability was found by Eugene Siegel in April 2025.

The second vulnerability (CVE-2025-62860) involved Bitcoin nodes that operate on the anonymous Tor network.

In fact, the Bitcoin Core developers revealed that thousands of reachable Bitcoin mainnet nodes had been granting permissions for incoming Tor connections.

Nevertheless, the issue did not affect nodes that do not use the optional whitelist configuration.

The three vulnerabilities are not new discoveries.

In fact, all of the issues were already fixed by the Bitcoin Core developers in October 2025.

The fixes were integrated into both Bitcoin Core 30.0, which was released on Oct. 10, and Bitcoin Core 29.2, rolled out on Oct. 14.

The high-severity mining vulnerability was also patched in Bitcoin Core 28.3.

The delay in the disclosure of the vulnerabilities was in line with the Bitcoin Core security policy, which usually calls for developers to wait at least two weeks after the end of life of the last affected software version before publishing details of medium- or high-severity vulnerabilities.
